entries.meaning: A specific illness that harms the body, often with a known cause. ---
examples: Heart disease runs in his family.
The vaccine wiped out a disease that used to kill thousands.
Doctors are still learning how these diseases spread.

entries.meaning: The state of being sick, or a particular sickness. ---
examples: She missed three weeks of work because of illness.
It started as a mild illness and turned into something serious.
Mental illnesses are far more common than people think.

entries.meaning: An illness caused by germs getting into the body. ---
examples: The cut got dirty and turned into an infection.
She is on antibiotics for a sinus infection.
Ear infections are really common in toddlers.

entries.meaning: A common viral illness with fever, aches, and a cough. ---
examples: Half the office is out with the flu.
I get a flu shot every October.
He came down with the flu right before the wedding.

entries.meaning: A mild illness that gives you a runny nose and a sore throat. ---
examples: I have had this cold for almost two weeks.
Do not kiss the baby if you are catching a cold.
Kids pick up six or seven colds a year.

entries.meaning: A body temperature higher than normal, usually caused by illness. ---
examples: She is running a fever of 102.
Give him this if the fever does not break by morning.
High fevers in small children can be scary.

entries.meaning: A sudden noisy push of air from the lungs. ---
examples: That cough has been hanging on since January.
He woke up with a dry cough and a sore throat.
Take something for the cough before bed.
entries.contrast: The gh is pronounced /f/ — cough rhymes with off, not with dough or through.

entries.meaning: A pain in the head. ---
examples: I have got a splitting headache.
Skipping coffee gives me a headache by noon.
Her headaches got better once she started sleeping more.
entries.contrast: The -ache ending is /eɪk/, never /eɪtʃ/ — HED-ayk.

entries.meaning: A pain in the belly. ---
examples: He stayed home from school with a stomachache.
That much ice cream will give you a stomachache.
She gets stomachaches whenever she is nervous.
entries.contrast: The ch in stomach is /k/ and the first vowel is /ʌ/ — STUH-muhk, not STOH-match.

entries.meaning: A small painful spot on the skin that is infected or has not healed. ---
examples: The bandage rubbed a sore onto his heel.
Cold sores always show up at the worst time.
Keep the sore clean and covered.

entries.meaning: An area of red, irritated spots on the skin. ---
examples: The antibiotic gave her a rash all over her arms.
That rash looks like poison ivy.
Diaper rashes clear up fast with the right cream.

entries.meaning: A harmful reaction of the body to something that is normally harmless. ---
examples: He has a peanut allergy, so read the label.
My allergies are brutal every spring.
Do you have any allergies we should know about?
entries.contrast: Stress moves in the adjective: AL-ur-jee, but uh-LUR-jik (allergic).

entries.meaning: A condition that narrows the airways and makes breathing hard. ---
examples: Cold air sets off his asthma.
She has had asthma since she was a kid.
Keep the inhaler handy in case the asthma flares up.
entries.contrast: The th is silent — AZ-muh, not AZ-thmuh.

entries.meaning: A disease in which abnormal cells grow out of control. ---
examples: Her mother beat cancer twice.
Smoking is the leading cause of lung cancer.
He was treated for cancer last spring.

entries.meaning: A serious infection that fills the lungs with fluid. ---
examples: The flu turned into pneumonia.
He spent a week in the hospital with pneumonia.
Pneumonia is especially dangerous for the elderly.
entries.contrast: The p is silent — noo-MOHN-yuh.

entries.meaning: Frequent, loose bowel movements. ---
examples: The medication gave him diarrhea for two days.
Travelers often get diarrhea the first week abroad.
Drink plenty of water if you have diarrhea.
entries.contrast: Spelled diarrhea in the US, diarrhoea in Britain.

entries.meaning: The sick feeling you get just before you might throw up. ---
examples: The nausea hit her about an hour after the treatment.
Take it with food to cut down on nausea.
He felt a wave of nausea on the boat.

entries.meaning: A sudden painful tightening of a muscle. ---
examples: I got a cramp in my calf halfway through the race.
She gets bad cramps the first day of her period.
Stretch it out and the cramp will pass.

entries.meaning: A dark mark on the skin where blood has collected after a blow. ---
examples: He came home with a nasty bruise on his shin.
The bruise turned yellow after a few days.
She had bruises up and down both arms.
entries.contrast: The ui is just /uː/ — BROOZ rhymes with cruise.

entries.meaning: An injury in which the skin is cut or torn open. ---
examples: The wound needed eight stitches.
Keep the wound dry for the first day.
Most of his wounds healed without scarring.
entries.contrast: The noun is WOOND; the identical spelling said /waʊnd/ (rhyming with found) is the past tense of wind.

entries.meaning: Physical harm done to the body. ---
examples: A knee injury ended his season.
She walked away from the crash with minor injuries.
The helmet prevented a much worse injury.

entries.meaning: An injury caused by heat, fire, or chemicals. ---
examples: He got a nasty burn from the oven rack.
Run cold water over the burn.
The burns on her hands took months to heal.

entries.meaning: A crack or break in a bone. ---
examples: The X-ray showed a hairline fracture.
She has a fracture in her left wrist.
Stress fractures are common among runners.

entries.meaning: An injury from twisting a joint too far. ---
examples: It is just a sprain, not a break.
He is out two weeks with an ankle sprain.
Bad sprains can hurt worse than fractures.

entries.meaning: The mark left on the skin after a wound heals. ---
examples: He still has a scar above his eyebrow.
The surgery left a thin scar.
Her scars have faded a lot over the years.

entries.meaning: A small bubble of fluid under the skin caused by rubbing or burning. ---
examples: My new boots gave me a blister.
Do not pop the blister or it will get infected.
She had blisters on both heels after the hike.

entries.meaning: An abnormal increase in the size of part of the body. ---
examples: Ice will bring the swelling down.
There is still some swelling around the ankle.
The swelling went away after a couple of days.

entries.meaning: A sudden loss of blood flow to the brain that damages it. ---
examples: Her grandfather had a stroke last year.
He is relearning to walk after the stroke.
High blood pressure raises the risk of strokes.

entries.meaning: A sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. ---
examples: He had a seizure in the parking lot.
The new medication cut her seizures in half.
Roll the person onto their side during a seizure.

entries.meaning: A mental illness marked by lasting sadness and loss of interest. ---
examples: She has been in therapy for depression since college.
Depression is not the same thing as a bad week.
Exercise helps his depression more than anything else.

entries.meaning: A strong, ongoing feeling of worry or fear. ---
examples: Flying gives him serious anxiety.
She takes something for anxiety before presentations.
Anxiety kept him up most of the night.
entries.contrast: The x sounds like /ɡz/ — ang-ZY-uh-tee, not ank-SY-uh-tee.

entries.meaning: A condition in which a person cannot stop using something harmful. ---
examples: He is in recovery from a painkiller addiction.
Addiction runs in some families.
The clinic treats all kinds of addictions.

entries.meaning: Ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep. ---
examples: Her insomnia got worse after the move.
He has tried everything for insomnia.
Caffeine after four o'clock guarantees insomnia.

entries.meaning: A severe headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light. ---
examples: She had to lie down in the dark with a migraine.
Bright screens trigger his migraines.
A migraine can knock you out for a whole day.
entries.contrast: Americans say MY-grayn; the British often say MEE-grayn.

entries.meaning: A raw sore in the lining of the stomach or on the skin. ---
examples: Stress did not cause the ulcer — a bacterium did.
He is on medication for a stomach ulcer.
Ulcers can bleed if they are left untreated.

entries.meaning: A lump formed by cells growing where they should not. ---
examples: The scan found a small tumor on her kidney.
Most breast tumors turn out to be benign.
Surgeons removed the tumor on Tuesday.
entries.contrast: Spelled tumor in the US, tumour in Britain.

entries.meaning: Redness, heat, and swelling in a part of the body that is hurt or infected. ---
examples: The pills bring down inflammation in the joints.
There is some inflammation in his throat.
Chronic inflammation damages tissue over time.
entries.contrast: The verb is inflame (in-FLAYM), but the noun shifts the stress: in-fluh-MAY-shuhn.

entries.meaning: A sign in the body that shows a disease is present. ---
examples: A dry cough was the first symptom.
Call us if the symptoms get worse.
She had every symptom except the fever.

entries.meaning: A set of symptoms that regularly occur together. ---
examples: Typing all day gave him carpal tunnel syndrome.
The syndrome was first described in the 1960s.
Several rare syndromes share the same gene.

entries.meaning: A fast spread of a disease through many people in one area. ---
examples: The city is dealing with an opioid epidemic.
A measles epidemic closed two schools.
Public health workers track epidemics in real time.

entries.meaning: A common childhood illness with itchy spots all over the body. ---
examples: Both kids got chickenpox the same week.
There is a vaccine for chickenpox now.
He was covered in spots from chickenpox.

entries.meaning: A condition causing pain and stiffness in the joints. ---
examples: Arthritis makes it hard for her to open jars.
He has had arthritis in his hands for years.
Cold weather makes the arthritis worse.

entries.meaning: A brain injury caused by a blow to the head. ---
examples: He got a concussion in the second quarter.
She is still recovering from a concussion.
Repeated concussions can cause lasting damage.
entries.contrast: Americans say get a concussion; the British usually say suffer concussion, with no article.

entries.meaning: Extreme tiredness that rest does not fix. ---
examples: Fatigue is the most common side effect.
She is dealing with constant fatigue.
The fatigue hit him around week three.
entries.contrast: French spelling, English stress: fuh-TEEG, ending in a hard /ɡ/.

entries.meaning: An uncomfortable feeling on the skin that makes you want to scratch. ---
examples: The cream stopped the itch right away.
I have got an itch right between my shoulder blades.
Bug bites leave an itch that lasts for days.

entries.meaning: A sudden, loud burst of air from the nose and mouth. ---
examples: One sneeze and the whole room said bless you.
Cover your sneezes with your elbow.
A single sneeze can travel across a room.

entries.meaning: A dull pain that lasts a while. ---
examples: There is a steady ache in my lower back.
The flu came with aches everywhere.
He felt a dull ache in his jaw.
entries.contrast: The ch is /k/ — AYK rhymes with cake, not with catch.

entries.meaning: A tiny organism that can cause disease. ---
examples: Wash your hands — germs are everywhere in daycare.
The wipes kill most germs on contact.
A single germ can multiply fast in warm food.

entries.meaning: A substance taken to treat illness, or the science of treating illness. ---
examples: Did you take your medicine this morning?
She is studying medicine at a school in Boston.
Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A drug prescribed to treat a condition. ---
examples: He is on three medications for his heart.
The medication made her drowsy.
Do not stop the medication without asking your doctor.

entries.meaning: A substance used as medicine, or an illegal substance taken for its effects. ---
examples: The drug is still waiting on FDA approval.
He was arrested on drug charges.
New drugs have made the disease survivable.

entries.meaning: A small solid piece of medicine that you swallow. ---
examples: Take one pill with breakfast.
She hates swallowing pills.
There is one pill left in the bottle.

entries.meaning: A flat, pressed piece of medicine. ---
examples: Dissolve the tablet in a glass of water.
Two tablets every six hours.
The tablet has a line down the middle so you can split it.

entries.meaning: A small container of medicine that dissolves in the stomach. ---
examples: Each capsule has 500 milligrams.
Swallow the capsules whole — do not chew them.
He opened the capsule and mixed it into applesauce.
entries.contrast: Americans say KAP-suhl; the British say KAP-syool.

entries.meaning: The amount of medicine taken at one time. ---
examples: Do not double the dose if you miss one.
The second dose comes three weeks later.
Kids get smaller doses than adults.

entries.meaning: A doctor's written order for a specific medicine. ---
examples: I need to pick up a prescription at the pharmacy.
This is prescription strength, not what you buy off the shelf.
She has three prescriptions to refill.
entries.contrast: A medical prescription, not a cooking recipe — Russian «рецепт» covers both, English does not.

entries.meaning: Medical care given to cure or manage an illness. ---
examples: She is starting treatment next Monday.
There are several treatments for this type of arthritis.
The treatment worked better than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: Treatment for a physical problem, or regular sessions with a counselor. ---
examples: He has been in therapy for about a year.
Physical therapy got her walking again.
New therapies are being tested right now.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: Medical treatment in which a doctor cuts into the body. ---
examples: She is having surgery on Thursday.
He needed surgery to repair the tendon.
Recovery from surgery took about six weeks.
entries.contrast: In American English you have surgery, with no article — not a surgery.

entries.meaning: A single act of surgery on a patient. ---
examples: The operation lasted four hours.
He has had two operations on the same knee.
It is a routine operation these days.

entries.meaning: Medicine put into the body with a needle. ---
examples: The injection stung for a second.
She gives herself injections twice a day.
One injection every three months keeps it under control.

entries.meaning: Shot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I am getting my flu shot tomorrow.
The baby is due for two shots at this visit.
It is just one quick shot in the arm.
They each did a shot of tequila.
Two shots of espresso, please.
He ordered a beer and a shot.

senses.head: The everyday American word for an injection, especially a vaccine
examples: I am getting my flu shot tomorrow.
The baby is due for two shots at this visit.
It is just one quick shot in the arm.

senses.head: A small serving of strong liquor or espresso drunk at once
examples: They each did a shot of tequila.
Two shots of espresso, please.
He ordered a beer and a shot.

entries.русский: укол, прививка; рюмка крепкого; порция эспрессо
entries.contrast: Americans get a shot; the British get a jab.

entries.meaning: A preparation that teaches the body to fight a specific disease. ---
examples: The vaccine is free at most pharmacies.
Two vaccines are approved for that virus.
A single vaccine can cover several strains.
entries.contrast: Americans stress the second syllable — vak-SEEN; the British say VAK-seen.

entries.meaning: The act of giving someone a vaccine. ---
examples: Bring your child's vaccination record.
Vaccinations are required before kindergarten.
She is overdue for one vaccination.

entries.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria. ---
examples: The doctor put him on antibiotics for ten days.
Antibiotics do nothing for a virus.
Finish the whole course of the antibiotic.

entries.meaning: A drug that reduces pain. ---
examples: They sent her home with a mild painkiller.
He is trying to get off the painkillers.
One painkiller took the edge off.

entries.meaning: A thick, greasy medicine that you rub on the skin. ---
examples: Put a little ointment on the burn.
The pharmacist recommended an antibiotic ointment.
Both ointments are available over the counter.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A strip of cloth wrapped around a wound. ---
examples: Change the bandage every morning.
She wrapped a bandage around his ankle.
There are clean bandages in the cabinet.

entries.meaning: Stitch has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cut took six stitches.
He goes back Friday to get the stitches out.
One stitch came loose overnight.
A few stitches came out along the hem.
She put in one more stitch and cut the thread.
The stitches on this bag are already coming apart.

senses.head: A loop of thread used to close a wound
examples: The cut took six stitches.
He goes back Friday to get the stitches out.
One stitch came loose overnight.

senses.head: One loop of thread made by a needle when sewing
examples: A few stitches came out along the hem.
She put in one more stitch and cut the thread.
The stitches on this bag are already coming apart.

entries.meaning: An operation that moves an organ from one body into another. ---
examples: He has been on the list for a kidney transplant for two years.
The transplant was a success.
Heart transplants are far more common than they used to be.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable — TRANS-plant; the verb is trans-PLANT.

entries.meaning: The process of putting donated blood into a patient. ---
examples: She needed a transfusion after the delivery.
Two transfusions got his levels back to normal.
The transfusion takes about three hours.

entries.meaning: Medicine that stops you from feeling pain during surgery. ---
examples: He was under anesthesia for two hours.
Some people feel sick coming out of anesthesia.
The dentist used local anesthesia.
entries.contrast: American spelling anesthesia; the British write anaesthesia.

entries.meaning: The process of getting well again after illness or injury. ---
examples: She made a full recovery.
Recovery from the surgery takes about a month.
The doctors called it one of the fastest recoveries they had seen.

entries.meaning: Something that makes a disease go away completely. ---
examples: There is still no cure for the common cold.
Researchers are hunting for a cure.
Some cures are worse than the disease.

entries.meaning: A treatment, often a simple or homemade one, for a minor problem. ---
examples: Honey and lemon is my grandmother's remedy for a sore throat.
Half these home remedies do not do anything.
The pharmacist suggested an over-the-counter remedy.

entries.meaning: A routine medical examination done when you are not sick. ---
examples: I have got a checkup on the fifteenth.
Kids need a checkup before the school year starts.
He skipped his checkups for five years straight.

entries.meaning: An arranged time to see a doctor or other professional. ---
examples: I have a doctor's appointment at ten.
Can I move my appointment to Friday?
She had three appointments in one week.

entries.meaning: A detailed medical image of the inside of the body. ---
examples: The scan came back clean.
They ordered a CT scan of his head.
Both scans showed the same thing.

entries.meaning: A photograph of the bones taken with special radiation. ---
examples: The X-ray showed a clean break.
They took X-rays of both hands.
You will get the X-ray results this afternoon.

entries.meaning: Temperature has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Let me take your temperature.
His temperature is up to 101.
Temperatures over 104 need a doctor.
Bring the butter to room temperature first.
Check the internal temperature with a thermometer.
Ovens hold temperatures differently, so watch the food, not the clock.

senses.head: How hot the body is, measured as a sign of health
examples: Let me take your temperature.
His temperature is up to 101.
Temperatures over 104 need a doctor.

senses.head: How hot or cold something is, measured in degrees
examples: Bring the butter to room temperature first.
Check the internal temperature with a thermometer.
Ovens hold temperatures differently, so watch the food, not the clock.

entries.contrast: Usually squeezed to three syllables in American speech — TEM-pruh-chur, not TEM-per-uh-toor.

entries.meaning: A natural substance the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy. ---
examples: She takes a vitamin every morning.
Vitamin D comes mostly from sunlight.
These vitamins taste like candy.
entries.contrast: Americans say VY-tuh-min; the British say VIT-uh-min.

entries.meaning: A pill or powder taken to add nutrients to the diet. ---
examples: He takes an iron supplement.
Most supplements are not tested the way drugs are.
Ask your doctor before starting a new supplement.

entries.meaning: A dangerous amount of a drug taken at one time. ---
examples: He survived an overdose last spring.
The ER treats overdoses almost every night.
An overdose of that painkiller can stop your breathing.

entries.meaning: The easing of pain or discomfort. ---
examples: The shot gave him instant relief.
She has had no relief from the headaches.
This cream promises fast relief from itching.

entries.meaning: Basic emergency treatment given before professionals arrive. ---
examples: Everyone on staff is trained in first aid.
There is a first aid kit under the sink.
She gave him first aid until the ambulance came.

entries.meaning: A place where sick and injured people are treated and stay overnight. ---
examples: They rushed him to the hospital.
She works nights at a children's hospital.
Two hospitals in the county closed last year.
entries.contrast: Americans say in the hospital; the British say in hospital, with no the.

entries.meaning: A place where people get medical care without staying overnight. ---
examples: There is a walk-in clinic two blocks from here.
The clinic opens at seven.
Free clinics fill up fast.

entries.meaning: A place where medicines are prepared and sold. ---
examples: The pharmacy closes at nine.
I will swing by the pharmacy on my way home.
Most pharmacies give flu shots now.

entries.meaning: An American store that sells medicine along with everyday goods. ---
examples: Grab some tape at the drugstore.
There is a drugstore on almost every corner.
Drugstores here sell everything from aspirin to greeting cards.
entries.contrast: American drugstore; the British say chemist's.

entries.meaning: A large room or section of a hospital for one type of patient. ---
examples: She was moved to the maternity ward.
Visitors are not allowed on that ward after eight.
The children's wards were full.

entries.meaning: A sudden situation that needs immediate medical help. ---
examples: Call 911 if it is an emergency.
They met in the emergency room at two in the morning.
The clinic handles minor emergencies.

entries.meaning: A vehicle that carries sick or injured people to the hospital. ---
examples: The ambulance got there in six minutes.
Two ambulances were already on the scene.
Pull over when you hear an ambulance.

entries.meaning: A trained worker who gives emergency care outside a hospital. ---
examples: The paramedics got his heart started again.
A paramedic checked her over at the curb.
He trained as a paramedic right out of high school.

entries.meaning: A doctor who performs operations. ---
examples: The surgeon said the tumor came out clean.
She is a heart surgeon at a teaching hospital.
Three surgeons were in the room.
entries.contrast: The -geon is /dʒən/ with a soft g — SUR-juhn, never SUR-gee-on.

entries.meaning: A formal word for a medical doctor. ---
examples: Check with your primary care physician first.
The hospital hired six new physicians.
Her physician recommended a specialist.
entries.contrast: A physician treats people; a physicist studies physics — different words, different jobs.

entries.meaning: A trained professional who treats mental or physical problems. ---
examples: She sees a therapist every other Tuesday.
The physical therapist gave him exercises to do at home.
Good therapists are booked months out.
entries.contrast: False friend: an American therapist is usually a counselor, while Russian «терапевт» means a general doctor — that is a physician.

entries.meaning: A doctor who treats children. ---
examples: Our pediatrician wants to see him again in a week.
She is looking for a new pediatrician.
Pediatricians see a lot of ear infections.
entries.contrast: Spelled pediatrician in the US, paediatrician in Britain.

entries.meaning: A medical doctor who treats mental illness and can prescribe drugs. ---
examples: A psychiatrist adjusted his medication.
It took two months to get in with a psychiatrist.
Psychiatrists go to medical school; counselors do not.
entries.contrast: The p is silent — suh-KY-uh-trist.

entries.meaning: A specialist in the mind and behavior who provides talk therapy. ---
examples: The school psychologist tested him for a learning disability.
She is a child psychologist.
Psychologists usually cannot write prescriptions.
entries.contrast: Silent p again — sy-KAH-luh-jist.

entries.meaning: A person trained to prepare and hand out medicines. ---
examples: Ask the pharmacist whether you can take these together.
The pharmacist caught a mistake in the dosage.
Pharmacists can give vaccines in most states.

entries.meaning: A trained person who helps women give birth. ---
examples: A midwife delivered both of her kids.
The midwife stayed the whole night.
Two midwives run the birth center.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: midwives (MID-wyvz), never midwifes.

entries.meaning: A doctor with expert training in one area of medicine. ---
examples: Your doctor can refer you to a specialist.
She saw three specialists before anyone figured it out.
The specialist ordered more tests.

entries.meaning: An arrangement in which a company pays part of your medical costs. ---
examples: Does your insurance cover physical therapy?
He lost his health insurance when the job ended.
Bring your insurance card to the appointment.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — say I have insurance, never an insurance.

entries.meaning: A chair on wheels for someone who cannot walk. ---
examples: He has been in a wheelchair since the accident.
The hotel has wheelchair access on every floor.
There were two wheelchairs parked by the entrance.

entries.meaning: A support that fits under the arm and helps you walk with an injured leg. ---
examples: She is on crutches for another two weeks.
One crutch slipped on the wet floor.
He hobbled in on crutches.

entries.meaning: A flat frame used to carry an injured person. ---
examples: They carried him off the field on a stretcher.
The stretcher would not fit through the door.
Both stretchers were already in use.
entries.contrast: Singular in English: a stretcher, even though Russian «носилки» is always plural.

entries.meaning: A tube with a plunger used to inject or draw out liquid. ---
examples: The nurse filled the syringe and tapped out the air.
Used syringes go in the red container.
He measured the dose with an oral syringe.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable — suh-RINJ, not SEER-inj.

entries.meaning: Needle has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looks away every time the needle goes in.
The needles are single-use.
It is a very fine needle — you barely feel it.
She threaded the needle on the first try.
There's a needle stuck in the pincushion.
Sewing needles come in different sizes.

senses.head: The thin sharp metal tube used to give an injection
examples: She looks away every time the needle goes in.
The needles are single-use.
It is a very fine needle — you barely feel it.

senses.head: A thin pointed metal tool with a hole for thread
examples: She threaded the needle on the first try.
There's a needle stuck in the pincushion.
Sewing needles come in different sizes.

entries.meaning: Thermometer has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Where is the thermometer? He feels warm.
The ear thermometer reads in two seconds.
We keep two thermometers in the medicine cabinet.
Stick a thermometer into the thickest part of the breast.
An instant-read thermometer is the best twenty dollars you'll spend.
Candy thermometers clip onto the side of the pot.

senses.head: A device that measures body temperature
examples: Where is the thermometer? He feels warm.
The ear thermometer reads in two seconds.
We keep two thermometers in the medicine cabinet.

senses.head: An instrument for measuring how hot something is
examples: Stick a thermometer into the thickest part of the breast.
An instant-read thermometer is the best twenty dollars you'll spend.
Candy thermometers clip onto the side of the pot.

entries.contrast: Stress is on the second syllable — thur-MAH-muh-tur, not THUR-moh-mee-tur.

entries.meaning: The instrument a doctor uses to listen to the heart and lungs. ---
examples: She warmed the stethoscope before putting it on his chest.
The stethoscope was still around her neck.
Medical students buy their own stethoscopes.

entries.meaning: Thin, loosely woven cloth used to cover wounds. ---
examples: Cover it with gauze and tape it down.
We are out of gauze — check the other kit.
The nurse pressed a square of gauze against the cut.

entries.meaning: A covering worn over the nose and mouth to block germs. ---
examples: The surgeon pulled down his mask to talk.
Masks are still required in the oncology wing.
She keeps a spare mask in her bag.

entries.meaning: A hole in a tooth caused by decay. ---
examples: The dentist found two cavities.
That cavity needs a filling.
Soda gave him cavities by the time he was ten.

entries.meaning: Metal wires fitted to the teeth to straighten them. ---
examples: She got her braces off last week.
Braces were the worst part of middle school.
His braces cost more than the car.
entries.contrast: Always plural in this sense — braces, never a brace for teeth.

entries.meaning: The practice of keeping clean in order to stay healthy. ---
examples: Hand hygiene cuts infection rates in half.
Dental hygiene starts before the first tooth.
Hygiene in the kitchen matters as much as in the clinic.

entries.meaning: The food a person usually eats, or a controlled eating plan. ---
examples: A balanced diet beats any supplement.
He has been on a low-salt diet since the heart attack.
Fad diets rarely last past February.
entries.contrast: In English diet usually means what you normally eat, not only a weight-loss plan.

entries.meaning: The process of getting the food the body needs to stay healthy. ---
examples: Good nutrition makes a real difference in recovery.
The label lists nutrition facts on the back.
Poor nutrition shows up in the bloodwork.

entries.meaning: The condition of carrying a developing baby. ---
examples: She felt great through the whole pregnancy.
Some medications are not safe during pregnancy.
Both pregnancies were textbook.

entries.meaning: A person who gives blood or an organ to someone else. ---

entries.meaning: The body's ability to resist a particular disease.
examples: The shot gives you immunity for about a year.
Immunity fades over time.
Kids build immunity by getting sick a lot.
